TALK TITLE: NEURO-INFORMED LEADERSHIP IN ACTION INTRODUCTION: This keynote weaves clinical understanding of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD) with lived experience and leadership practice to illuminate how PAE quietly shapes women’s health and workplace functioning across the lifespan. Alcohol‑related brain differences in planning, memory, impulse control, emotional regulation, and social understanding are rarely diagnosed yet frequently misinterpreted as inconsistency, laziness, or defiance. From the outside, such women may appear fully capable; from the inside, leadership and daily work can feel like running on 5% battery with ten apps open or trying to drive with one foot on the gas and one on the brake. The session explores how these invisible injuries interact with anxiety, depression, trauma, and other comorbidities, creating a heavy “hidden load” that affects performance, confidence, and self‑perception. AIM: This is not a scientific research talk. My aim is to equip women leaders to recognize and respond wisely to the often‑invisible impacts of prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE) and other neurodivergence's in themselves and those they lead, reframing “problem staff” as those with brain‑based differences that call for compassion, accommodation, and neuro‑informed leadership rather than shame. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This keynote uses a narrative and knowledge-translation approach, combining clinical understanding of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD) with lived experience and leadership practice to explore how prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE) may affect cognitive functioning and workplace performance. Clinical insights and literature on FASD and neurodiversity Lived-experience reflections and leadership scenarios Neuro-informed leadership and workplace inclusion frameworks The session integrates conceptual discussion, narrative examples, and practical leadership strategies to help leaders recognize invisible brain-based differences and apply compassionate, neuro-informed approaches in professional settings. RESULTS: The keynote highlights that prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE) and related neurodevelopmental differences can affect women’s leadership, wellbeing, and workplace functioning in often invisible and misunderstood ways. These brain-based differences are frequently misinterpreted as poor performance or lack of motivation. By applying neuro-informed leadership approaches, including compassion, awareness, and supportive accommodations, leaders can reduce stigma, improve workplace understanding, and create more inclusive environments where individuals can perform and thrive. CONCLUSION: By challenging behavior‑only interpretations and introducing self‑compassion, mindfulness, and practical accommodations, this talk offers women leaders a neuro‑informed framework for supporting themselves and their neurodivergent employees. Participants will learn to ask “What is this behavior telling me about capacity and wiring?” rather than “What is wrong with this person?”, and will leave with concrete strategies for designing roles, feedback, and workplace cultures that allow people who are wired‑differently to contribute their best. Ultimately, the keynote invites a shift from managing “problem staff” to cultivating sustainable, humane, and inclusive leadership that honors diverse brains. KEYWORDS: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders; prenatal alcohol exposure; neurodiversity; women’s leadership; women’s health; workplace inclusion; executive functioning; self‑compassion; mindfulness; accommodations. TALK TITLE: BEYOND SOFT SKILLS: THE BIOLOGY OF FUTURE-READY LEADERSHIP INTRODUCTION: Modern leadership environments reward constant availability, high cognitive output, and emotional labor. Many high-performing professionals — particularly women — operate in chronic stress states while remaining highly functional. Over time, the body can adapt to persistent stress hormone exposure, reducing conscious stress perception while physiological strain continues. Chronic stress and insufficient recovery, including poor sleep quality, are associated with reduced decision confidence, impaired cognitive flexibility, and decreased emotional regulation. AIM: This talk explores how biological stress mechanisms influence leadership performance and long-term health, with particular relevance for high-achieving women balancing professional leadership with emotional and family responsibilities. It introduces biological self-regulation, recovery competence, and physiological awareness as essential future skills for sustainable high performance. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The talk integrates current findings from stress physiology, neuroscience, and behavioral science, combined with applied leadership performance diagnostics. Many clients begin with a structured web-based biological screening that generates a personalized performance and stress profile. Common indicators include sleep disruption, decision fatigue, reduced recovery capacity, and cognitive overload. Based on this assessment, leaders are supported through structured mentoring focused on physiological regulation, recovery optimization, and sustainable performance strategies. RESULTS: By increasing biological awareness and strengthening the ability to regulate our internal responses, individuals can make more stable and thoughtful decisions even under pressure. It supports greater mental clarity and focus, allowing people to stay present and productive. This awareness also builds resilience, helping individuals recover more effectively from stress and challenges. Over time, these skills contribute to consistent, sustainable performance in both personal and professional environments. CONCLUSION: Future-ready leadership requires integrating biological literacy with traditional leadership competencies to sustain performance without compromising long- term health. KEYWORDS: Women in Leadership; Stress Physiology; Biological Resilience; Future Skills; Sustainable Performance; Sleep and Leadership; Self-Regulation BIOGRAPHY: Dr. Doris Bell, PhD is a biologist, toxicologist, and Energy Mastery Coach working at the intersection of science, self-leadership, and sustainable high performance. TALK TITLE: UNSTOPPABLE VOICES: BEING A DISRUPTOR FOR GOOD! INTRODUCTION: Disrupting entrenched systems is often perceived as conflict, rebellion, or professional risk, which discourages many individuals from challenging the status quo. A common misconception suggests that meaningful change can only be initiated by those who hold formal authority. However, systemic inequities and structural barriers continue to persist when individuals hesitate to question established norms. In modern institutional and professional environments— especially with the growing resistance to equity-focused initiatives such as Gender Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (GEDI)—there is an increasing need to reframe disruption as a constructive and responsible leadership practice. In this session presented by Cate Thomas, disruption is explored as a strategic approach to leadership that enables individuals at any level to challenge inequities and foster meaningful institutional change. AIM: The aim of this presentation by Cate Thomas is to reframe disruption as a constructive leadership strategy and demonstrate how individuals—regardless of formal authority—can challenge systemic barriers and drive inclusive, sustainable change. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This presentation adopts a conceptual and reflective methodology grounded in intersectional and adaptive leadership frameworks. It integrates theoretical perspectives from social justice, leadership studies, and inclusion practices with professional experiences in advocacy, education, and institutional reform. Through reflective discussion, case-based insights, and real-world professional scenarios, the session explores practical strategies for constructive disruption. The approach emphasizes understanding positionality, engaging stakeholders, confronting privilege, and addressing structural barriers while navigating contemporary challenges such as the backlash against GEDI initiatives. RESULTS: The discussion highlights that disruption, when applied thoughtfully and strategically, can serve as an effective leadership tool for organizational and systemic transformation. Findings indicate that individuals at all levels of an organization can influence change by recognizing their positionality, building collaborative relationships, and addressing institutional barriers. The approach reframes disruption from conflict to purposeful leadership, encouraging open dialogue, critical reflection, and the advancement of justice, equity, diversity, and inclusion. CONCLUSION: Disruption should not be viewed as rebellion or professional risk but rather as a constructive and necessary leadership practice. By applying intersectional and adaptive leadership principles, professionals can challenge inequitable systems while maintaining collaboration and professional integrity. Empowering individuals to become “disruptors for good” enables organizations to move beyond compliance-based inclusion toward meaningful and lasting systemic change. KEYWORDS: Disruption for good; Adaptive leadership; Intersectionality; Systemic change; Justice, equity, diversity, and inclusion (JEDI); Organizational leadership; GEDI initiatives. TALK TITLE: MASTER CREDENTIALED COACH AND CEO OF @CHOICE COACHING &CONSULTING LLC INTRODUCTION: Modern professional women—particularly women of color—are navigating an impossible intersection of excellence and exhaustion. Conditioned by generational survival and societal scripts like the 1978 Enjoli “do-it-all” ideal, they wear invisible capes of over-responsibility, perfectionism, and chronic self-betrayal. This talk exposes the hidden toll of this conditioning—what I call the cost of the cape—through both data and lived experience. AIM: To illuminate the psychological, physiological, and cultural costs of Superwoman Syndrome among high-achieving,primary-breadwinning women—and to introduce the DIVA Breakthrough Experience™ as a holistic framework for sustainable success rooted in nervous system fluency, alignment, and embodied leadership. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Drawing from Dr. Cheryl Woods-Giscombé’s Superwoman Schema research,WHO’s wellness model, and data from my own coaching practice, my signature DIVA Breakthrough Experience Framework—Discovery, Inspiration, Vitality, and Alignment—was applied as a qualitative and quantitative intervention. TALK TITLE: “THE POWER WE DON’T NOTICE” INTRODUCTION: Emotional intelligence (EQ) is widely recognized as a critical leadership capability that can be developed over time. While leaders often focus on core EQ components such as self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and relationship management, one important factor that influences all of them is power. Every leader holds a certain level of actual or perceived power, which shapes team dynamics, communication, trust, and engagement. However, many leaders are not trained to understand or consciously manage their power in everyday interactions. Recognizing how power operates within leadership roles is essential for building trust, psychological safety, and stronger organizational relationships. AIM: This talk focuses on helping leaders become more aware of the power they carry in their roles, whether it comes from their position, expertise, experience, or personal influence. Many leaders use power unconsciously without fully understanding how their words, decisions, and behaviors affect others. By recognizing the different forms of power they hold and understanding how it is perceived by team members, leaders can better manage their interactions and build stronger relationships. The session also highlights how leaders can intentionally adjust the way they use power in different situations to strengthen emotional intelligence, enhance trust, create psychological safety, and ultimately improve team collaboration and performance. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The presentation draws on leadership experience, practical frameworks, and real-world organizational insights to help leaders better understand how power operates within leadership roles. Through reflective discussions and practical leadership scenarios, the session encourages participants to examine their own leadership styles and recognize how their actions and communication influence team dynamics and trust. By exploring different sources of leadership power—such as authority, expertise, and personal influence—the session helps leaders understand how power affects relationships and team engagement. It also highlights how leaders can intentionally adjust their approach in different situations to build trust, promote psychological safety, and strengthen overall team performance. RESULTS: Understanding and intentionally managing leadership power plays a vital role in strengthening emotional intelligence and building effective team relationships. Leaders hold various forms of power, such as authority, expertise, and influence, and the way they use this power significantly impacts how teams communicate, collaborate, and perform. When leaders use their power with awareness and positive intent, they create environments built on trust, openness, and psychological safety, where team members feel respected and confident to share ideas and contribute fully. This approach encourages stronger collaboration, higher engagement, and improved performance. However, when power is used unconsciously or in a controlling manner, it can damage trust, limit communication, and reduce team motivation. By becoming aware of how their power affects others and adjusting their leadership approach accordingly, leaders can strengthen relationships, enhance emotional intelligence, and foster healthier, more productive team cultures. CONCLUSION: Power is often an overlooked yet highly influential element of emotional intelligence in leadership. While leadership development commonly emphasizes communication, empathy, and self-awareness, the role of power in shaping relationships and team dynamics is frequently underestimated. Every leader holds some form of power—whether through authority, expertise, experience, or personal influence—and this power significantly affects how others respond, communicate, and engage within a team. When leaders are unaware of how their power impacts others, it can unintentionally create barriers to open communication, reduce trust, and weaken team relationships. However, when leaders become conscious of the power they hold and understand how it is perceived by those around them, they can begin to use it more thoughtfully and intentionally. This awareness enables leaders to balance authority with empathy, encourage open dialogue, and create environments where team members feel valued, respected, and psychologically safe to contribute their ideas and perspectives. By learning to apply power responsibly rather than avoiding it, leaders can strengthen trust, foster healthier team cultures, enhance collaboration, and ultimately drive higher levels of engagement, performance, and meaningful leadership outcomes. KEYWORDS: Emotional Intelligence, Leadership Power, Trust, Psychological Safety, Leadership Development, Team Culture, Organizational Leadership, Relationship Management. Talk Title: “Scaling Humanity: The Leadership Shift Behind Sustainable Global Growth.” INTRODUCTION: Sustainable global growth demands more than financial capital, infrastructure, or technological advancement—it requires a leadership shift that places humanity at the center of economic progress. Across developing and emerging economies, entrepreneurs hold immense potential to drive innovation, job creation, and long-term resilience, yet many remain excluded from global opportunity due to systemic barriers such as limited market access, fragmented ecosystems, and inequitable investment practices. As global economies become increasingly interconnected, leadership must evolve to foster inclusive entrepreneurial environments that enable participation across borders, cultures, and industries. Ethical investment, digital platforms, capacity building, and public–private collaboration are no longer optional mechanisms; they are essential enablers of sustainable development. When aligned effectively, these forces empower entrepreneurs not only to scale economically, but also to generate positive social and environmental outcomes. Scaling Humanity: The Leadership Shift Behind Sustainable Global Growth explores how human-centered leadership and globally connected ecosystems can unlock entrepreneurial potential while strengthening economic resilience. By examining strategies, challenges, and scalable frameworks, this work highlights how leaders and institutions can align capital, policy, and innovation to support entrepreneurship that advances prosperity, equity, and long-term global impact. AIM: The aim of this presentation is to examine leadership-driven frameworks that enable sustainable and inclusive entrepreneurial growth across global markets. It seeks to identify actionable strategies that empower entrepreneurs, reduce systemic barriers, and align stakeholders—governments, investors, institutions, and private-sector leaders—around shared economic and human-centered outcomes. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This work employs a mixed-methods approach, integrating: Literature review of thought leadership and recent research in global entrepreneurship Comparative case studies from 2–3 regions (e.g., Latin America, Africa, Southeast Asia) Interviews or surveys with entrepreneurs and ecosystem actors Analysis of policy frameworks and investment trends This methodology enables both contextual depth and practical scalability across diverse economic ecosystems. RESULTS: Findings indicate that entrepreneurial ecosystems grounded in ethical investment, capacity building, and global market access produce measurable economic and social benefits. Key outcomes include increased job creation, higher income levels, improved innovation and technology diffusion, and enhanced resilience to economic shocks. The research also highlights successful support models—such as incubators, export facilitation, digital tools, and cross-sector collaboration—that enable entrepreneurs to scale sustainably while maintaining social and environmental stewardship. CONCLUSION: Scaling humanity alongside economic growth is not only possible—it is essential. This framework demonstrates that leadership rooted in inclusion, ethics, and global collaboration can transform entrepreneurship into a catalyst for long-term, sustainable development. By aligning policy, capital, and innovation with human-centered values, leaders can foster ecosystems that generate prosperity while advancing global equity, resilience, and shared opportunity. TALK TITLE: CREATING A LIVING LEGACY: YOU MAKE A DIFFERENCE AND THE STORY OF YOUR LIFE EXPERIENCE HAS AN IMPACT INTRODUCTION: In contemporary society, where productivity, speed, and measurable achievement dominate cultural values, gratitude is often misunderstood as a passive or sentimental emotion. However, emerging psychological and neurological research suggests that gratitude functions as a powerful cognitive strategy that enhances resilience, emotional regulation, and overall well-being. Dr. Dan Rubin, drawing from decades of professional experience and personal reinvention later in life, proposes that gratitude is not merely a reaction to positive circumstances but an intentional mindset capable of transforming how individuals perceive aging, success, and legacy. By reframing life experiences through gratitude, individuals can shift their focus from what is missing to what is meaningful, creating a renewed sense of purpose and influence across generations. AIM: The aim of this keynote study is to explore how the intentional practice of gratitude can: 1.Enhance psychological resilience and emotional well-being. 2.Improve mental clarity and focus. 3.Strengthen interpersonal relationships and social connection. 4.Encourage individuals—particularly older adults—to transform life experiences into meaningful contributions and living legacies. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This work is based on a conceptual and experiential framework combining: Psychological and neuroscientific research on gratitude, resilience, and cognitive reframing. Narrative methodology, utilizing storytelling and lived experiences from Dr. Dan Rubin’s life and career. Audience engagement techniques, including reflective questions, humor, and guided exercises that help participants identify personal values and meaningful life experiences. Practical gratitude frameworks, such as daily reflection practices, real-time cognitive reframing strategies, and legacy-building tools designed to help individuals document and share their stories. The keynote integrates qualitative insights from decades of teaching, mentoring, and leadership development, as well as observational feedback from diverse audiences including professionals, seniors, and leadership communities. RESULTS: Participants exposed to the gratitude-focused framework demonstrated several key outcomes: Improved emotional resilience, as gratitude practices helped interrupt negative thought patterns and reframe setbacks. Enhanced mental clarity and focus, resulting from intentional attention to meaningful experiences. Stronger interpersonal connections, as gratitude fostered appreciation and empathy in relationships. Renewed sense of purpose, particularly among older adults who began to view their experiences as valuable sources of wisdom and influence. Increased motivation to share personal stories, leading to the creation of “living legacies” that extend beyond individual achievements. These results suggest that gratitude functions not only as an emotional response but also as a cognitive and behavioral strategy for personal transformation. CONCLUSION: Gratitude is far more than a positive emotion—it is a powerful psychological tool capable of reshaping perception, strengthening resilience, and enriching human connection. When practiced intentionally, gratitude enables individuals to move beyond a deficit-focused mindset toward one centered on meaning and contribution. Dr. Dan Rubin’s framework demonstrates that purpose and significance do not diminish with age; rather, they expand as individuals learn to transform their experiences into wisdom that benefits others. By embracing gratitude as a daily practice, individuals can cultivate vitality, deepen relationships, and consciously create a living legacy that continues to inspire future generations. KEYWORDS: Gratitude, Psychological Resilience, Aging and Purpose, Cognitive Reframing, Living Legacy, Meaningful Living, Personal Development, Emotional Well-being, Leadership, Intergenerational Influence. TALK TITLE: LEADERSHIP WITHOUT CERTAINTY - WHEN THE OLD ROLE IS GONE AND THE NEW ONE ISN’T BUILT YET. INTRODUCTION: We often talk about leadership as confidence, clarity, and having a plan. But real life doesn’t always give us that. Career transitions are one of those moments - when the old role has ended, the new one isn’t here yet, and you still feel pressure to show up like everything is normal. In this talk, I bring lessons from high-risk maritime operations, where uncertainty is part of the job and decisions still have to be made. The point is simple: uncertainty isn’t a personal flaw. It’s a leadership condition - and you can learn how to lead through it Aim: This session is designed to give participants a practical, repeatable way to lead themselves through change without rushing into the next thing, burning out, or losing confidence along the way. The goal is to help participants make better decisions even when the picture isn’t complete, rebuild momentum through small proof and progress, and use community and visibility in a way that creates real opportunities. So the next chapter doesn’t just “happen” to them - they shape it. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The talk follows a clear, experience-based structure built around a three-part framework: Clarity → Capability → Community. I will share real examples, a few simple tools (including a one-sentence transition narrative participants can use immediately), and a short interactive exercise called the Transition Command Brief—a five-line template that turns reflection into action. This is not therapy, and it’s not motivational fluff. It’s practical leadership: decisions, behaviours, and small systems that make progress feel steady again. RESULTS: By the end, participants should feel more confident talking about transition, more grounded in what to stop and what to build, and more capable of turning uncertainty into forward movement. We will look at why transitions so often stall: identity attachment, fear-based choices, isolation, and the lack of “proof” that you’re moving in the right direction - and how this framework helps reduce those traps with structure, evidence, and support. I will also show how leadership practices from complex environments - safety, compliance, incident learning - translate surprisingly well into personal reinvention. CONCLUSION: Leadership without certainty isn’t about having the perfect answer. It’s about creating stability while the future is still taking shape. With Clarity (aligned decisions and boundaries), Capability (skills plus proof), and Community (support plus contribution), attendees will leave with language and a simple plan they can use right away. KEYWORDS: Leadership without certainty, Career transition, Identity shift, Reinvention, Decision-making under ambiguity, Resilience, Confidence rebuilding, Change management, Clarity, Boundaries, Upskilling, Capability building, Small wins / proof of progress, Personal branding / transition narrative, Visibility. TALK TITLE: NADA–ALZHEIMER PROTOCOL — “I AM THE WRITER OF MY OWN STORY” INTRODUCTION: ONE WORLD, ONE PEOPLE, ONE NATION = ALZHEIMER It is as if someone knew 5 million years ago that in our time Alzheimer’s would dominate the world, and therefore ensured in advance the ARHGAP11-B gene as a rescue for those affected (it stimulates the multiplication of stem cells, creating new neurons). It is said that a new era is coming — one government, one country, one people, one language. Looking into the future through Alzheimer’s, patients become those who do not know who they are, do not recognize anyone, do not know language, and do not know their origin — young, old, men, women. Alzheimer’s is still often equated with dementia. This research shows that there is a difference between dementia and Alzheimer’s (AB), which can be demonstrated through examinations: NADA‑m, NADA‑m + contrast, and NADA‑c. AIM: To provide a different approach to Alzheimer’s through the NADA‑Alzheimer Protocol by understanding the balance between ARHGAP11‑A and ARHGAP11‑B genes and allowing the brain to regenerate itself to prevent plaque formation and maintain stability. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Conceptual research and clinical observation using diagnostic approaches such as NADA‑m, NADA‑m with contrast, and NADA‑c, with a focus on gene balance and neuron regeneration (mirror neurons). RESULTS: Alzheimer’s appears as a protective mechanism enabling neuron regeneration. The research suggests that balancing ARHGAP11‑A and ARHGAP11‑B genes may help control Alzheimer’s progression. Younger patients (18+) show different healthcare utilization patterns compared to older populations. Current treatment methods may cause severe side effects such as strokes and brain swelling, indicating the need for alternative approaches. CONCLUSION: Alzheimer’s is no longer limited to people aged 65+, but may appear from age 18 onward. The NADA‑Alzheimer Protocol offers a new perspective focused on brain self‑regeneration and gene balance. It also emphasizes the need to differentiate Alzheimer’s from dementia and to improve communication with patients through all stages of brain degeneration. KEYWORDS: Alzheimer’s disease, dementia differentiation, ARHGAP11 genes, neuron regeneration, mirror neurons, brain health, neuroprotection, mobile medicine, Alzheimer’s protocol. BIOGRAPHY: Nada Marić is a licensed nurse and licensed dental assistant with a research interest in Alzheimer’s (A) and (AB). Many women begin to experience persistent fatigue, sleep disruption, weight changes, brain fog, and reduced stress tolerance. These symptoms are frequently misunderstood as burnout or poor time management. As a result, women apply the same productivity, nutrition, and fitness strategies that worked in their 20s and early 30s. However, these strategies often stop working and can even increase stress and exhaustion. AIM: This keynote aims to bridge the gap between health and performance by increasing awareness of the biological drivers of energy and productivity after 35. TALK TITLE: “HO-ME-I-KU” PHILOSOPHY, WHICH MEANS “PRAISE EDUCATION” INTRODUCTION: The concept of self-care has gained significant prominence in today’s society as individuals increasingly confront complex demands that affect their holistic health. In Cameroon, women often carry significant responsibilities which expose them to chronic stress, and is usually accompanied by persistent challenges of gender-based-violence, financial insecurity, cultural expectations of resilience and limited access to mental health services. In Cameroon, women often shoulder multiple and intersecting responsibilities within their families, workplaces, and communities, placing them at heightened risk of chronic stress and emotional exhaustion. AIM: This paper was aimed at exploring how self-care practices contribute to a healthier life. Specifically, this work examined the extent to which mindfulness meditation and regular sleep contributes to a healthier life. while regular and sufficient sleep supports cognitive functioning, emotional balance, and physical health. Together, these self-care practices are presented as essential components of a holistic approach to maintaining and improving overall quality of life. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Participants included sixty women ages 30 to 50years all chosen from church community groups in Buea, South West Region Cameroon. A one-group pre- test, post-test quasi experimental design was used. A pre-test was administered followed by a six weeks counselling interventions on self-care practices (1 hour weekly) with church community groups. Following the pre-test, participants engaged in a six-week counseling intervention focused on self-care practices. The intervention was delivered through structured weekly sessions lasting one hour each and was facilitated within the church community group settings. RESULTS: Findings revealed a significant difference in the pre and post-test scores. On average, the variability of the scores was significantly higher after post-test (M=14.93, SD=3.22) than during pre-test (M=12.22, SD=3.50), t =.001. This indicates the difference during pre and post-test was significant and represents a substantial effect of counselling interventions on mindfulness . On average, the variability of the scores for regular sleep was significantly higher after post-test (M=13.73, SD=3.24) than during pre-test (M=16.45, SD=3.01), t =.011. As stated by Milovidov (2020), women need to practice regular sleep in order to live healthier CONCLUSION: Similarly, regular and adequate sleep is essential for emotional regulation, cognitive performance, hormonal balance, and physical restoration. When practiced consistently, these self-care behaviors contribute to improved mental health, increased resilience, and a higher quality of life, underscoring their importance as foundational components of women’s overall well-being.This work reinforces the belief that true wellness begins within and extends outward to communities, animals, and the planet. Through intuitive healing, conscious guidance, and the global support of The Wellness Universe, individuals are empowered to live healthier, more authentic lives while contributing to collective well-being and global harmony. This work supports conscious healing and holistic well-being, creating a positive ripple effect for individuals, communities, and the planet. KEYWORDS: self-care practices, mindfulness, mindfulness meditation, regular sleep, healthy sleep patterns, sleep hygiene, mental well-being, psychological health, emotional well-being, physical health, stress reduction, stress management, holistic health, healthy lifestyle behaviors, preventive health. She is passionate about promoting a dynamic Africentric approach to counselling that reflects local realities, cultural values, and community strengths. The B.I.O.N.I.C. Team (Believe It Or Not I Care) initiative was created to empower students to support one another and build caring school cultures that reduce isolation and promote emotional well-being. AIM: This presentation aims to demonstrate how the B.I.O.N.I.C. Team model empowers students to create supportive peer networks that help prevent bullying, suicide, and social isolation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The keynote presentation will utilize prepared slides, real-world experiences, and interactive audience engagement. Programs such as “Prevent Bullying by Just Saying H.I.” promote kindness and peer support, fostering safer learning environments. Talk Title: “Leading with Lightness: Reclaiming Playfulness as a Strategic Strength in Modern Leadership” INTRODUCTION: In today’s rapidly evolving and uncertain world, leadership is frequently associated with pressure, constant responsibility, and the risk of burnout. However, one of the most overlooked capacities of effective leadership is lightness—the ability to remain curious, adaptive, and human while navigating complexity and change. Drawing on insights from positive psychology, neuroscience, and leadership development, this presentation introduces the concept of light leadership, where playfulness becomes a strategic strength rather than a distraction from productivity. Through reflective storytelling and research-based insights, the session explores how cultivating playfulness can enhance resilience, inspire authentic connection, and stimulate innovation within teams and organizations. AIM: This presentation aims to explore how playfulness can be integrated into leadership practices to strengthen emotional agility, creativity, and resilience. The session seeks to redefine leadership lightness as a sign of strength and provide practical strategies for leaders to incorporate curiosity, joy, and playful intelligence into communication, decision-making, and team culture. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This presentation adopts a multidisciplinary and reflective–experiential approach, integrating positive psychology, neuroscience, coaching frameworks, and leadership development research. Participants will engage with storytelling, micro-reflection exercises, and guided dialogue designed to demonstrate how playful states influence perception, emotional regulation, and decision-making. Real-life case studies from executive coaching and organizational leadership development programs will illustrate how playfulness contributes to psychological safety, collaboration, and adaptability. The session emphasizes embodied learning, allowing participants to experience how lightness can be consciously integrated into everyday leadership practices. RESULTS: Findings from applied coaching practice and leadership development programs indicate that introducing playfulness as a conscious leadership strategy significantly improves team engagement, creativity, and resilience under pressure. Leaders who cultivate a light and curious mindset report stronger interpersonal trust, more open communication, and increased collaboration across organizational hierarchies. Playfulness also functions as a cognitive and emotional reset, reducing perfectionism and encouraging experimentation. These outcomes demonstrate that lightness and joy are not contrary to productivity; rather, they are powerful catalysts for sustainable performance, innovation, and meaningful human connection in organizations. CONCLUSION: “Leading with Lightness” reframes leadership as a dynamic process rooted in curiosity, compassion, and creative problem-solving rather than stress and control. By integrating playfulness into leadership culture, organizations can foster environments where innovation, well-being, and purpose coexist. This session invites leaders to embrace play not as something separate from leadership but as a deeply human capacity that supports adaptability, resilience, and authentic leadership in times of change. This presentation explores how redefining success through The New Rules of Midlife Leadership can empower women to sustain energy, confidence, and high performance through hormonal transition and beyond. Practical micro-strategies such as energy audits, reset rituals, and intentional decision-making become the foundation for a leadership style that values balance as much as achievement. This work reframes midlife not as a limitation, but as a strategic turning point where wisdom, awareness, and adaptability create long-term leadership success. The New Rules of Midlife Leadership empower women to evolve how they lead, less from depletion and more from alignment. Women leaders, particularly in service-oriented sectors such as healthcare, education, and nonprofit leadership, often face heightened risk due to the added burden of invisible emotional labor and organizational pressures. Addressing burnout therefore requires approaches that strengthen both leadership capacity and internal resilience. AIM: To demonstrate how strengthening leadership capabilities through the Grit & Grace Leadership Model can help women leaders reduce burnout, enhance resilience, and improve decision-making, communication, and professional support systems. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This workshop uses the Grit & Grace Leadership Model, which has three main parts to help leaders reduce burnout and become more resilient. Growth Powered Partners encourages leaders to create strong support networks for guidance and encouragement. RESULTS: Application of the Grit & Grace Leadership Model supports leaders in shifting from reactive to intentional leadership behaviors. CONCLUSION: Leadership development functions not only as professional growth but also as a critical mental health support strategy. By strengthening personal agency, communication skills, and collaborative partnerships, leaders can mitigate burnout risks, regulate stress responses, and sustain their impact over time. Intentional leadership practices therefore serve as a protective factor that enables leaders to remain resilient, effective, and purpose-driven. TALK TITLE: CULTIVATING SELF-AWARE AND RESILIENT LEADERSHIP IN COMPLEX ORGANIZATIONAL ENVIRONMENTS: AN INTEGRATIVE COACHING-BASED FRAMEWORK INTRODUCTION: The study contributes to leadership theory by reframing resilience not as a fixed trait but as a dynamic, developable capacity rooted in self-awareness and intentional practice. It challenges traditional performance-centric paradigms by highlighting the limitations of high achievement without reflective awareness, emphasizing that sustained leadership effectiveness requires internal alignment as much as external competence. Furthermore, integrating coaching methodologies with decision-making frameworks such as the OODA Loop demonstrates how leaders can operationalize self-awareness into actionable strategies, enabling continuous adaptation in volatile environments. The findings underscore the necessity of embedding reflective practices within leadership development programs and suggest that organizations should prioritize human-centric, psychologically informed approaches to cultivate future-ready leaders. AIM: This keynote aims to explore how emotional resilience functions as a critical mechanism for transforming human consciousness, bridging the gap between psychological insight and behavioural change in leadership, relationships, and holistic well-being. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This study/article is based on leadership coaching practices, resilience frameworks, executive leadership experiences, and transformational development strategies shared through professional insights, case studies, and global leadership engagements. Qualitative observations and reflective leadership methodologies were applied to explore self-awareness, resilience, decision-making, and sustainable leadership growth. RESULTS: Findings indicate that self-awareness functions as a critical enabler of conscious leadership, directly influencing decision-making quality, emotional regulation, and relational effectiveness. Leaders who actively cultivate self-awareness demonstrate: Enhanced adaptability in ambiguous and high- pressureenvironments, Improved team engagement through empathy-driven communication, Greater alignment between personal values and organizational goals, and reduced burnout through intentional reflection and boundary-setting The SCCR framework emerged as a robust model for developing resilience, with each dimension contributing uniquely: Self-awareness enables insight into internal drivers and blind spots, Compassion fosters psychological safety and trust, Curiosity promotes learning and reframing of challenges, and Resourcefulness supports agile problem-solving and innovation. CONCLUSION: This presentation introduces a framework for embodied and conscious leadership that prioritizes human connection, authenticity, and relational safety in work environments. Participants will leave understanding that leadership excellence exists on the other side of inner work—it is a state of being, not merely a set of skills. KEYWORDS: Self-aware leadership; resilience; executive coaching; adaptive leadership; SCCR framework; decision-making; organizational behavior; leadership development.
